sections.text: An 18-20-minute read, depending on your pace.
The recent events that have shaken the country are truly nightmarish.

Nightmare is the only word that comes close, and even it is not enough. A nightmare is something you wake up from; you open your eyes and the danger dissolves with the dark. This does not dissolve. We wake up every morning, and it is still there, waiting for us in the news.

It comes to us in headlines first. Another body found. Another family shattered. We read it with our tea still hot on our way to work, school, while the country carries on as if a day is a day. And the people in those headlines had days. They had plans, and people who loved them, and children who waved goodbye at the door without knowing it was the last one.

The country is shaken because the fear does not stay where the crime happened. A mother in a town she has never left reads about a woman in a town she has never seen and feels it in her chest as if it happened on her own street. We carry the grief of strangers because we know, with a dread we do not always say out loud, that it could be our daughter, our sister, our mother. And when it can be any of us, the events stop being separate. They become one long thing. A pattern. A truth about where we live that we have not yet found the words to face.

Someone made a decision that they are going to take the lives of innocent people. It is more than a crime issue because this entity is not looking to gain anything monetarily, but to violate the existence of innocent people. I keep coming back to the word decision. It matters. This was not an accident, not a moment of rage that got out of hand. Somewhere, somehow, a choice was made. A plan was formed. And a plan can be repeated, passed down, learned, so the horror is not a once-off, it is a method, and a method does not stop on its own.

I also keep coming back to innocent, and I do not use it carelessly. It means the women were not targets because of what they did. They were targets because of what they are. Nothing they could have said, worn, done, or avoided would have changed the outcome, because the decision existed before they were even in the room. That is what separates this from the crimes we have learned to understand. Crime, the way we usually speak about it, wants something. It wants money, possessions, revenge, a score settled, a point made. We can arrange it in our minds, however ugly the arrangement, because there is a logic to it. But when there is nothing to gain, the logic collapses, and we are left holding something we have no shape for.
No money. No property. No score. Nothing was being taken from these women, except everything.

So, I reach for entity, because entity is the only word that does not force me to give the thing a single face. A man I could understand in the terrible sense of arranging him into a story, what made him, what hardened him, what he did. But this thing is bigger than one man. It moves through families, through the places where women are meant to be safe, through the silences of institutions. It is a belief and a permission. It teaches that a woman's existence is a resource, and a resource can be used up.

And when the aim is existence itself, the violation is complete. It is not enough that she dies. She is made to be gone. Erased. So that the fear she carried becomes an inheritance for her daughter, and the grief an inheritance for everyone who loved her. The entity does not only take the life. It takes the life and leaves the fear behind, to do the rest of its work for us.

That is why I say it is more than a crime. Crime ends at the law. This is trying to end something else entirely, striking directly at the lives of those who were all daughters, sisters, mothers, and partners. Murdered

They were all daughters. Somewhere there is a parent who will never be the same, a parent whose heart now has a shape missing from it. A daughter is supposed to outlive the people who raised her; that is the quiet promise every family carries. These parents are living with proof that the promise can be broken.
They were all sisters. Somewhere there is a sibling who shared their childhood, who fought with them and laughed with them and knows exactly what was taken from them.

They were mothers. Somewhere there are children who said goodbye at the door not knowing it was the last time. They will grow up measuring every milestone against an absence, and every parent killed is a childhood interrupted, a whole future of advice, comfort, and reassurance that will never arrive.
They were partners. Somewhere there is someone who chose them and was chosen, who planned a life with them, who knew the way they laughed, who now wakes on one side of an empty bed.

And the list does not end there. They were colleagues, teachers, grandparents, aunties, grandmothers, neighbours, friends of friends, the woman in the next pew, the one you stood behind in the queue, the woman who loved running, and so many more. Every single one was a whole person with a whole world inside her, people who loved her, and days she had already planned.
But before any of that, they were simply women. Women who woke up that morning with no idea, women who had every right to believe the day would just be a day.

And then the last word arrives, the one that undoes everything: Murdered. Not died, because dying can be innocent, an accident, an illness, the body's own quiet failure. Murdered is a decision. Murdered is a hand. Murdered is the word that tells the truth, that these lives did not end, they were taken.

Faced with this reality, the people we depend on once again do not have solutions. They release statements, condolence messages, and so on, and with every statement, another heartbeat stops. Once again. That is the word I cannot escape. This is not their first failure, and they know it, and we know it, and still every time we hold out a tired sliver of hope, and every time it is spent.

They release statements. Condolence messages. Words, in other words. And words cost nothing, which is precisely the point, because what we need from them is not words. We need the next body not to be found. We need the mothers to come home. We need them to have done their job years ago. Instead, we get the ritual of grief, performed beautifully, performed sincerely, performed by people who will go home to their own locked doors afterwards.

And the terrible irony in the sentence: with every statement, another heartbeat stops. It is as if the two are connected, as if the statement and the death are synchronised. The words go out to comfort the last loss, and while we are reading them, the next one is already happening.

A statement is a headstone delivered in advance. It marks the death it cannot prevent. The more fluent it is, the more we are meant to feel heard, and the less anything changes. Condolence is what you offer when you cannot bring the person back. It is an admission, dressed up as comfort, that the people we trusted to protect us could not and did not.
The people we depend on once again do not have solutions. And the tragedy is that we have stopped being surprised.
This leaves us with the enduring question: what is the solution to this tragedy?
Not the response for one news cycle. Not another statement, another promise, or another message of condolence after another life has been lost. What would actually stop this?

What would make women feel that the people and systems around them are not simply waiting to mourn them? What would allow children to grow up without learning that a parent can disappear from an ordinary day? What would make families believe that the next headline will not contain someone they love?
None of us truly know because we do not even know what this is.

We know the outcome. We know that innocent people are losing their lives. We know that families are being destroyed and that fear is spreading through communities. But we do not know how to hold the thing itself in language.
Is it crime? Is it hatred? Is it power? Is it entitlement? Is it the failure of institutions? Is it all these things at once?

Perhaps part of the problem is that we keep asking for one name when what we are facing is made up of many connected failures. We want one explanation, one cause, one person or institution to blame, because a single answer would make the tragedy easier to understand.

But what we are witnessing does not feel simple. It is not only the moment when a life is taken. It is everything that comes before it, everything that allows the danger to grow, and everything that follows afterwards, when the country expresses shock but continues as before.

And because we cannot agree on what to call it, we keep responding to fragments. One person speaks about violence. Another speaks about gender. Someone else speaks about policing, poverty, social breakdown, or the failure of families. Each conversation may be pointing towards something real, but the argument over which truth should come first becomes another way of avoiding the whole truth.
The uncertainty is not weakness. It is what remains when the people with authority do not have an answer. But not knowing cannot become permission to stand still.

The fact that we cannot yet name the whole problem does not make the bodies less real, the fear less real, or the responsibility less real. If anything, it makes the urgency greater. We may not know the complete solution, but we know that what is happening cannot continue to be treated as normal. Another statement cannot be the final response to another death.
Yet, while the question remains open and unanswered by those who should know, a second wound opens up: as a people, we start turning on each other because of a multitude of factors.

This is the second wound, and we do it to ourselves. The first wound is delivered by whoever takes the lives; the second is the one we inflict on one another in the aftermath. The entity is not even in the room, and still, we tear at each other.

There are the women, fuelled by uncertainty and fear. And their fear is not theoretical. It is waking up and reading that another body has been found. It is walking to the car with the keys already in hand. It is looking at every man who shadows too close. Fear like that must go somewhere. It becomes a demand for answers, for safety, for someone to say this will not happen again. And when the demands are not met, they harden into grief, and grief hardens into fury. The women are not looking for a fight. They are looking for anyone to finally hear them.

Then there are the men, feeling attacked and becoming contrarians. Because a demand aimed at "men" lands on every man, including the ones who have never raised a hand. And when someone who has done nothing is told that their whole category is under suspicion, the first instinct is not reflection, it is defence. You push back because you feel accused of a crime you did not commit. You argue the generalisation because it feels unjust. And the more the argument heats up, the less anyone is listening, and the contrarian position hardens into a shield, until the actual deaths get lost behind the argument about who is allowed to feel accused.

And finally, the middle ground, either silent or playing both sides. These are the ones who choose comfort, or safety, or who genuinely do not know whose side to take, so they take none. They keep their heads down, they say nothing, or they say a little something to each camp so neither turns on them. But silence in this climate is not neutrality; it is absence. The women do not hear you. The men do not hear you. The dead especially do not hear you. You are not keeping the peace; you are simply not standing anywhere, and that is exactly what makes the middle ground so costly, because it is the largest group, and it does nothing.

It is not one group turning on another. It is everyone turning on everyone. Women angry at a world that fails them, men defensive at being blamed for it, and the middle quietly drifting, waiting for it all to blow over.
And the whole time, the entity is still working. We are so busy arguing about who is at fault that the one who actually picks them off is not even the focus of the room.

If gender wars are always going to be the result, then we have to really reflect on what is important to us. There is a prediction built into that cycle: we have seen this before, and we can now say it out loud that we will see it again, because nothing in our responses seems to change the ending. And if we can predict the result, then we have to ask why we keep playing towards it.
Is it being right, or is it protecting our people?

Being right is cheap. It costs nothing to win an argument. You marshal your points, you find your evidence, you get the satisfaction of a reply that lands, and you go to bed still holding your position, warm in the knowledge that you were correct, while the women are still being picked off.

Protecting is expensive. It asks you to put down the argument, to move past the need to win, to do the unglamorous, unending work of keeping people safe. It rarely gives you the satisfaction of a clean victory, because protection is not measured in points scored but in lives kept safe, and a life kept safe looks like nothing happening at all.

So, the real question is not who is right. The real question is what we are spending our days on while the entity works. Being right or wrong in the end does not change the fact that, while we are arguing, this entity is picking off our sisters. Rightness does not shield them. A well-won debate does not hold a door for a woman walking home. The argument may comfort us, but it does not protect her, and protection is the only thing that costs anything here.

And I am not saying truth does not matter. We need to name things accurately or we will fix the wrong things. But naming is meant to serve saving. When naming becomes a substitute for saving, when the debate itself becomes the whole of what we do, we have quietly chosen being right over protecting, whether we admit it or not.

This often leads to the familiar deflection: "Yes, men die too." I want to sit with that sentence, because it is the one some people will not let you say. The moment you mourn the women, someone answers that men die too, as if grief were a rationed resource, as if honouring one loss meant stealing from another. And they are right that men die too. They are simply wrong to say it in that way, as a correction, as if the two losses competed for the same heart.

Both exist in the same place, at the same time. The same country. The same streets. The same systems that fail to protect anyone. Violence does not draw a neat line and kill only one kind of person. It is messy, and it claims more than one group, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of blindness.

But there is a difference in the shape of it, and I will not pretend otherwise. Men die in violence, plenty of them, and every death is a tragedy that deserves the same mourning. But these women are being killed in a pattern that targets their womanhood itself. The threat follows them into the places they are supposed to be safe. That is a different fear. And both things can be true at once: men die too, and women are being picked off for being women.

If we truly want to change any of them, we actually have to change them, not argue about them. You cannot fix the violence against women by winning a point about men, and you cannot fix the violence against men by proving women are not the only victims. Change does not happen in the comment section. It happens when the conditions that allow both kinds of violence stop being tolerated, and that requires all of us, not just the ones who feel most accused.

Being a contrarian does not really matter now. There will always be someone whose identity depends on being against whatever the room believes, someone who answers every motion with the opposite, not because it is true but because it is the opposition. And contrarians save nobody. They do not calm a single fearful woman. They just keep the argument alive so that the argument never has to become action.

To share with my brothers and sisters: "all men" and "not all men" do not change the fact that we have a problem in our hands. "All men" is unfair, because it indicts the innocent. "Not all men" is true, because it is true. And neither sentence moves the problem one inch. You can argue forever about which one is the fairer verdict, and the whole time the problem sits in our hands, waiting for us to decide whether we are going to hold it or pass it along.

It will not make women less fearful just because you are not those men. Your innocence is real, but it does not travel. It does not walk behind a woman on an empty street. It does not reassure her when she hears footsteps. She does not know that you are not those men, and even if she did, one exception does not undo a pattern. Fear does not negotiate with statistics; it does not read your character reference and relax. So telling a woman "not all men" is not comfort. It is a request that she stop being afraid so that you can feel better about yourself.

The only thing that makes women less fearful is a world where those men stop existing, and that is not an argument, it is a job, and it belongs to all of us, especially to the ones who are not those men.
Because ultimately, it is up to us to protect each other.

Not the people we depend on, who release statements. Not the ones who are busy being right. Us. The ones reading this. You and me. That is where responsibility lands, whether it is fair or not, because the institutions have proven they will not carry it and the arguments have proven they cannot.
Protect each other. Not just the women, though especially the women. Each other. Because fear and anger have divided us, but division is not a strategy, it is a surrender.

And protect the next generation. The children who said goodbye at the door. The ones not yet born who will inherit either our wisdom or our trauma. They do not get to choose what we hand them, so we have to choose for them. That is the whole weight of being the ones who came before. We can be the ones who pass down fear, or the ones who pass down something else.

We must try to deny them the trauma. I keep coming back to that word, deny, because it is strange and it is right. Trauma can be refused. It is not fate; it is an inheritance we can choose not to collect and not to deliver. The fear a mother carries does not have to become the fear her daughter carries. The grief does not have to become a child's first lesson about the world.

Because they should know how precious life is. That is the point of denying them the trauma. We are not protecting them so they can live in fear of death; we are protecting them so they can live as if life is the beautiful, fragile thing it is. A childhood that is not interrupted by loss teaches what no lecture can: that life is worth guarding, worth living, worth handing on.

Regardless of biological, social, economic factors, and so on. A life is a life, precious in the same measure, whether the woman was rich or poor, young or old, from this town or that. The entity does not check your category before it decides you are a target. We should not need a category before we decide you are worth protecting.

This means we must recognise that a protest to a protest only keeps us stagnant in the long run. Water that is stagnant is not moving, and it is also not clean; it breeds. That is what a protest-to-a-protest produces: not motion, but stagnation. And out of stagnation comes the same thing again, the next argument, the next headline, the next name.

Every response that exists only to counter the last response leaves us in the same place. She says this, so he says that. He says that, so she says the other. Each round feels like movement because the noise is loud, but the position of the room never changes, and neither does the ground the entity walks on. A protest against a protest is not a movement. A movement has a direction. It has people leaving the argument behind and going somewhere. The question is not whether we are louder than whoever shouted last, but whether we are closer to making the next body not be found.
Even these words that I jot down do not change the world. They do not bring those souls back.

There is a heaviness to admitting that, but the admission is not defeat, it is honesty, and honesty is the beginning of everything else. Words alone do not change the world. But the world is changed by people moved by words, and you cannot hand someone the resolve to act without first handing them something that stirs it.

There is something else the words do, and it is not small. They mark that someone noticed that someone refused to scroll past another body being found, that in a country which can be silent, one voice said the names out loud. The dead do not hear it, we know that, but the living do. A woman reading this learns she is not alone in the fear. A man reading this learns that being one of the not-those-men means more than saying it.
So no, the words do not change the world. But they are not nothing. They are the part of the work that happens in the dark, before the part of the work that happens in the light.
And most importantly, let us never forget the women whose lives were lost.

Never forget. Because forgetting is the quiet way the cycle continues. When the names stop being repeated, the deaths stop being real, and when the deaths stop being real, the next one costs less. Remembering is not decoration; it is resistance. Every time we say a name, we refuse to let the woman become a statistic the country has already moved on from.

Let these names be the reason we strive for change. That is the task you have given us. Not that we should feel sad, though we should. Not that we should post and forget, though we often do. But that the names should be the engine. When the work is slow and the hope is thin, we look at the names and remember what the work is for. A name is a why. A list of names is a why that will not let you stop.

A sentence that runs from one name to the next, and the distance between them is measured in the very thing this piece cries out against. Between the past and the present, there are more names, so many that you could not fit them all into one breath, and that is the indictment. Each one was somebody's daughter, sister, mother, partner. Each one had a day planned. Each one deserved to be the last name on the list.

And the hope hidden in that sentence is this: we go back through the past, all the way to the present, still saying them. The names survive the attempt to erase their owners. And if the names survive, then the women have not been erased, and the fight to keep any new name from joining the list is still ours.
I thank you. And God bless.
